en.title: Chatbots make news readers more confident, but not more accurate
paras: People who use AI chatbots to check whether news stories are true become more confident in their judgments, but not more accurate, according to a new study by researchers at a large public university. The results suggest that relying on AI for fact-checking may weaken a skill that people need when the AI is wrong.

The team recruited 600 adults and showed each of them 20 short news stories. Half of the stories were real and half were fabricated. One group could ask a chatbot about each story before deciding; a second group could search the web; a third group had no help at all.

Participants who used the chatbot rated their confidence much higher than those in the other groups. However, their accuracy was only slightly better than that of the group with no help, and lower than that of the web-search group. When the chatbot gave a wrong answer, which happened in about one of every eight stories, most chatbot users simply accepted it.

"People treated the chatbot like a calculator," says the study's lead author. "They stopped looking for clues in the story itself, such as the source or the date." The researchers compare this effect to the way some drivers lose their sense of direction after years of using GPS.

The authors note that the study used a single chatbot and only English-language stories, so the results may not apply to other tools or languages. They also did not measure whether the effect lasts over time.
Still, they recommend that AI fact-checking tools show their sources and admit uncertainty. "If the tool says 'I'm not sure' when it is not sure, people keep thinking," the lead author explains.

en.title: Robots learn kitchen tasks better in imperfect virtual worlds
paras: Training robots in a perfect virtual kitchen may not be the best way to prepare them for a real one. A team of engineers has found that robots trained in simulations with small, deliberate imperfections, such as slightly wrong object weights or flickering lights, perform better when they are moved to real homes.

Robots usually learn household tasks in simulation because it is cheap and safe: a virtual robot can drop thousands of plates without breaking anything. The problem is that the real world never looks exactly like the simulation, and robots often fail when small details change. Engineers call this the "reality gap."

To narrow the gap, the researchers created 1,000 versions of the same virtual kitchen. In each version, they randomly changed details like the friction of the countertop, the color of the cups and the position of the camera. A robot arm was then trained to load a dishwasher in all of these kitchens.

When the arm was tested in five real kitchens, it completed the task 81 percent of the time. A similar arm trained in a single, perfect simulation succeeded only 46 percent of the time. "Variety taught the robot what not to pay attention to," says one of the engineers. "The color of a cup does not matter; its shape does."

The approach has a cost. Training in many kitchens took about three times longer than training in one. The team is now testing whether a smaller number of carefully chosen variations could give similar results.
The researchers believe the method could help robots in other settings, such as warehouses and hospitals, where conditions change constantly.

en.title: Teaching language models to admit what they don't know
paras: Large language models often answer questions with the same confident tone whether they are right or wrong. A new training method aims to change that by teaching models to say how sure they are, and to say "I don't know" when the evidence is weak.

Overconfidence is one of the main causes of so-called hallucinations, answers that sound plausible but are false. Because users cannot easily tell a correct answer from a hallucination, confident mistakes can be more harmful than honest uncertainty.

In the new method, the model is rewarded not only for correct answers but also for confidence estimates that match its real accuracy. If the model says it is 90 percent sure, it should be right about nine times out of ten. Answers given with high confidence that turn out to be wrong receive a large penalty.

The researchers tested the approach on a set of 5,000 questions about science and history. Compared with the original model, the trained model answered with false confidence 40 percent less often, while its overall accuracy stayed almost the same.

"We didn't make the model smarter; we made it more honest about its limits," says the lead researcher. She adds that this could make AI assistants safer in areas such as medicine and law, where a wrong answer can have serious consequences.
However, the team warns that users may find a model that frequently says "I don't know" less useful, and that the method has so far been tested only on short factual questions.

en.title: Smarter scheduling could cut the energy cost of training AI
paras: Training a large AI model can consume as much electricity as hundreds of homes use in a year. A group of computer scientists has developed a scheduling system that could reduce the environmental impact of that energy use by up to 30 percent without delaying results significantly.

Data centers usually run training jobs as soon as computers become available, regardless of how the electricity is produced at that moment. The new system, instead, predicts when the local power grid will have more solar and wind energy and moves flexible jobs to those hours.

Not every task can wait. The system separates jobs into two types: urgent jobs, such as answering users' questions, which always run immediately, and flexible jobs, such as training new models, which can be delayed by a few hours.

In a six-month test at a university data center, the system reduced energy drawn from fossil-fuel sources by 30 percent and lowered the electricity bill by 12 percent. Training jobs finished, on average, only 15 minutes later than before.
"Most people think saving energy means using less computing," says one of the authors. "We showed that it often just means using it at the right time."

The researchers admit that the gains depend on the region. In places where the grid has little renewable energy, there is less room to shift jobs. They plan to share the system as open-source software so that other data centers can test it.
